en: Three generations of Kyrgyz had slaughtered them.
To this Kakan who had settled here,
If we consider what those versed in lore say,
They came after making entreaties,
One cauldron for every household hearth,
They gave it, saying, “Make your living.”
Unable to endure his wrath,
The medicine called Közün struck,
And Kakan's people remained there.
The punishment and affliction of Qin Shi,
He had handed him over into powerful hands.
His wrath had been fierce,
For what these Kyrgyz had done,
Against Kakan of the forty Chinese tribes,
I am Börök of Beijing,
Of the great people of the forty Chinese tribes,
They had challenged his rule.
Upon the guilty men, by God,
A deed that was not forgotten had occurred,
Those supporters said to have fought,
Had formed countless hosts.
Their warriors had been like steel,
The blood of those who contended was spilled.
The solitary died, living souls died,
Soulless livestock died,
They committed an immense deed,
You did not fear the men,
Digging out their lives, you laid them straight,
You committed an unforgettable deed.
Cutting down those men,
He cut down the heroes and uprooted them,
What these Kyrgyz intend to do,
Will not be forgotten even when broken apart.
They are no people who wander idly,
Their temper is keen, with poison-like force,
These pressing Kyrgyz are no ordinary people.
I received news from the Kyrgyz,
From the Kyrgyz Khan Beken arose,
His spirit surging from his valor,
The thoroughbred he rode was itself heroic,
No land could hold them firmly,
There are no people like these in what they do,
That great one, they say, was a Kyrgyz,
When anger spoke, do not strike and break,
He was born, they say, among the Kyrgyz,
When he thrust like a ball, he took the prize,
By night he broke through and made a road,
Without delay he attacked the people,
One of understanding, they say, from the Kyrgyz.
The champion went straight against him,
Of the many souls who faced him,
They saw a place from which none returned.
Before long, so many souls,
Sat there having perished.
When one looks, such was the calamity.
Thus, among the Kyrgyz who stood there,
Know that his strength had wearied,
He drove them on, striking at their ranks,
Toward Sarkaluu’s settlement,
Come on, striking through the raid,
Great Beijing, the mighty people, fell into disorder,
If you see the shepherd, look at his coat,
Its warriors were exceptional,
Every man had recovered,
The unruly villain who acknowledged no leader,
Returned again to his place,
His people mounted up and went to war,
The people of Beijing—True Heaven,
He has honor, and his venom is strong,
That army is dense as a mountain.
When his frenzy seizes him,
The eighteen thousand worlds,
He has the might to lay waste.
He becomes a scourge upon the people,
When his furious demon seizes him,
The eighteen thousand worlds,
Drawing breath like a dragon,
The beastly world rises in enmity.
The encampment of everyone he encountered,
I shall be Chyng Temir.
The eighteen thousand worlds,
If he gathered and seized them wholesale,
I shall drive them on and exact tribute.
If my fury rises and I strike with a curse,
Would the black mountain not be shattered?
If a stark command comes from the khan,
Would its onslaught not find them?
When the Mongols stood in Beijing,
Would he not exact tribute from a whole world?
If you stiffen in anger,
The four corners of the world,
The five quarters you have marked out,
Would they not be smashed to pieces?
When I become Chyng Temir,
Scorching until the sands were swept up,
When rejoicing, he was no mere common man,
The valleys shook and mountains fell,
My valiant one knew it.
As the age approached its end,
Thus he came to Kakan,
Saying the enemy would not take what was given,
He was destined for great dominion.
Saying this, Chyng Temir,
Angrily gathered an army,
When he gathered troops, he gathered a multitude,
Those younger than fifty-five,
Let not a single old soul remain,
Those who had passed eighteen,
The roll of the young men,
Saying not one youth should remain behind,
Kakan, root and branch,
He gathered them all together.
From the elder side came grievous slaughter.
He had cast the people into a dispute.
Their wits bewildered, their heads aching,
He had cast the people into turmoil,
He did not stand by and watch in vain,
An extraordinary upheaval, a great conflict,
The people were ruined and the nation grieved,
An extraordinary affliction, a great conflict,
The people rose and began to assemble.
Of what the Kalmyk had given,
Of what had long been increasing since ancient times,
The Kyrgyz asked grimly.
A wrathful scourge began.
The people cried out and tumult arose,
When they looked, nothing caught the eye,
The people stirred in a great upheaval,
Its sorrow could not be discerned,
They gathered an army for the contest,
They gathered the whole host in great numbers.
Together they stood in Kongol,
The affliction that threw the people into panic,
How the True Lord had measured it,
Such was the command he gave.
The great Chinese nation cried aloud,
They had witnessed their khan’s wrath,
Stricken by its warrior,
The brave Eren, Khan Esen,
Sat burdened with worry,
While the people cried out in distress,
As he was about to take up his decree,
His wrath became known to the people,
A merciless ordeal began,
Even their livestock were plundered,
All the people found no refuge,
Asking what this khan’s decree might be,
The populace cowered in fear,
The wise among them marveled,
The witless did not understand,
Bewildered by milk and kumis,
The people stood pale with longing.
Chyng Tengir was indeed a mighty lord,
Kakanchy and Beijing were his support,
Not merely Beijing, but the whole world—
The time had come for him to rule it,
A true mainstay of the world,
The time had come for him to become one.
A sage, accomplished in stratagems,
Even the black scourge could not escape
Those who knew the extent of their cunning,
From the inspector who roamed the land,
From the dark eye of calamity,
From the dark eye of the scourge,
With doors open and belts loosened,
The dear people living at ease,
Making them move as though within a bend,
